column3: Near-verbatim parallel: lasting righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and hope than wealth and children.
The nearby passage declares that none can find refuge apart from Allah, grounding His exclusive guardianship.
It identifies the final outcome as belonging to the God-conscious, supporting the focus's claim about the best end.
Near-verbatim parallel: lasting righteous deeds are better with the Lord in reward and final return.
Allah alone has unseen knowledge, no one is protector apart from Him, and none shares His judgment.
The surrounding declaration that truth is from the Lord and that choices have consequences frames the parable's outcome.
A defeated faction at a named place offers only a general image of reversal after apparent strength.
The immediate context rejects worldly adornment and commands steadfast devotion, anticipating the garden owner's collapse.
Those who patiently seek their Lord's face receive the good final outcome of the abode.
Its reference to testing and shaking believers at that point is not materially linked to divine guardianship or reward.
The companion attributes all power to Allah while correcting the garden owner's confidence in his possessions.
Allah's emphatic proclamation of truth supports the focus's designation of Him as the True One.
At that point every soul is tested by what it sent ahead and returned to Allah, its true Master.
The immediately preceding ayah states that no supporting party could help the garden owner apart from Allah.
It presents an evil alliance ending in enduring punishment, a broad counterpart to the focus's concern with final outcome.
Judgment belongs only to Allah, who relates the truth and is the best of deciders.
The nearby promise that Allah does not waste the reward of righteous work prepares the focus's best-reward declaration.
The Inevitable names the ultimate reality that vindicates truth, though it does not address guardianship directly.
The defeat and humiliation of the magicians' side supplies a general scene of decisive reversal.
The garden owner's wrongful confidence that his garden will never perish begins the error resolved in the focus.
Angels announce that patient believers have attained the excellent final outcome of the abode.
It calls patience better for the patient, offering a limited parallel to the focus's divine preference for the better end.
The nearby description of believers' gardens concludes that theirs is an excellent reward and resting place.
It calls attention to the final outcome of those warned, without the focus's exclusive divine-protection theme.
Allah promises not to waste any worker's deed and describes His own reward as the best reward.
The garden owner falsely expects a better return to his Lord, directly contrasting the focus's true best outcome.
Believers know the Hour is the truth, connecting divine truth with the eschatological end.
The cry for destruction in Hell at that place has only a remote verbal overlap with the focus.
This opens the two-garden parable whose collapse culminates in the focus's declaration of Allah's guardianship.
It calls the revelation truth from the Lord and contrasts belief with the Fire-bound rejection of it.
Those given knowledge declare Allah's reward better for believers who act righteously and remain patient.
The garden owner's boast in greater wealth and a stronger following is precisely overturned by the focus.
Allah's word becomes binding upon disbelievers that they are companions of the Fire, a general final-outcome link.
Moses joins reliance on Allah with patience and explicitly states that the final outcome belongs to the God-conscious.
The flourishing gardens establish the visible prosperity later shown unable to secure the owner.
The Lord's forgiveness and painful punishment are broad background to recompense but lack a close connection.
Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah, supporting His sole authority without the focus's outcome language.
The garden's destruction and the owner's remorse over associating partners immediately lead into the focus.
It identifies what comes from the Lord as truth, but does not develop exclusive guardianship or recompense.
Its contrast between inferior and better provisions is too distant from the focus's reward and final outcome.
The companion confronts the garden owner's disbelief in the Creator, forming part of the direct corrective dialogue.
Its use of the word truth concerns the people of Lot's improper desire, not the focus's divine guardianship.
All might belongs to Allah, reinforcing that ultimate authority and protection are His alone.
The companion affirms Allah as his Lord and rejects associating anyone with Him, directly anticipating the focus.
It explicitly calls the end of a people's affair loss after they tasted its evil consequence.
It contrasts taking low worldly gain with the better hereafter for the God-conscious.
Allah's parable contrasts transient falsehood with what benefits and remains, clarifying the victory of truth over appearance.
It states that a reward from Allah is better for those who believe and fear Him.
Allah is strong and mighty, supporting the focus's attribution of decisive authority to Him.
The punishment becomes due after collective denial of messengers, a general instance of an inevitable outcome.
Allah knows who brings guidance and who will have the final outcome of the abode; wrongdoers do not prosper.
Its detailed instruction to record debts justly uses truth and guardianship in a legal context unrelated to the focus.
The messenger brings good news and warning in truth, a broad and indirect connection to recompense.
It rejects taking protectors besides Allah, whose supposed mediation cannot replace devotion owed to Him alone.
It describes disbelievers disputing with falsehood to undermine the truth, in the same surah's surrounding warning.
When Allah wills harm none can repel it and people have no protector apart from Him.
It concerns denial of a confirming revelation even though it is truth, without a close outcome or guardianship link.
Moses's fear at the staff-sign is unrelated to the focus beyond Allah's power in a broad sense.
The hereafter and final outcome are assigned to those who do not seek worldly elevation or corruption.
The eternal promise of Allah is truth, connecting truth to enduring reward.
Concealing known truth is a general ethical failure rather than a close parallel to the focus.
Allah gives both worldly reward and the beautiful reward of the hereafter to those who do good.
It emphatically calls the stated reality the truth of certainty, without developing the focus's protection or reward.
The first life and the Hereafter both belong to Allah, establishing His control over the final state.
The difficult ascent is only a lexical and moral echo, not a direct statement of the best outcome.
Allah is your Protector and the best of helpers, a direct parallel to His true guardianship in the focus.
It calls the commanded direction truth from the Lord but otherwise concerns ritual orientation.
People are returned to Allah, their true Master; judgment belongs to Him alone.
The question whether Abraham brought truth or play is too indirect despite the truth vocabulary.
The companions of Paradise have a better resting place, a limited recompense parallel.
It asks readers to consider the outcome of plotters whose scheme and people were destroyed.
The Hereafter is explicitly declared better and more enduring than worldly life.
The delayed acknowledgement that Moses brought truth concerns an unrelated command.
Ibrahim receives good in this world and is among the righteous in the Hereafter, broadly joining present and final good.
It affirms the reality of the Fire-dwellers' dispute, with no close relation to divine guardianship.
It calls kind speech and forgiveness better than charity followed by injury, a narrow ethical use of better.
Former peoples stronger in power were seized for sins and had no protector against Allah, closely echoing failed worldly strength.
The command to give relatives and the needy their due is only distantly related through material wealth.
It directs attention to the outcome of criminals after punishment, a generic final-consequence parallel.
Allah is the true King and sole deity, a concise affirmation of the ultimate authority named in the focus.
It treats Allah's promise and the Hour as truth, framing disbelief in the coming final reckoning.
Allah alone deserves praise, possesses judgment in both worlds, and is the one to whom all return.
The denial that Allah's true promise of resurrection will occur is relevant only at the broad eschatological level.
Allah is the True, while what is invoked besides Him is false, directly supporting the focus's exclusive truth claim.
Allah is the true Lord, and after truth there is only error, a close theological formulation.
The Lord's provision is better and He is the best provider, a partial parallel to His being best in reward.
Even when believers are empowered, the final outcome of all affairs belongs to Allah.
Allah is the True and whatever is invoked besides Him is false, closely paralleling the focus's declaration.
The Messenger brings guidance and the religion of truth that Allah will make prevail over all religion.
Allah is the True, gives life to the dead, and is capable of all things, grounding the final reversal.
Allah chooses whom to favor from His great bounty, with only a broad connection to reward.
The true call belongs to Allah alone, while appeals to others receive no answer.
Failing to take the difficult ascent does not specifically concern the focus's guardianship or recompense formula.
Knowing that revelation from the Lord is truth is contrasted with blindness, a general truth parallel.
Showing Ibrahim the dominion of the heavens and earth supplies only a broad basis for certainty in Allah's rule.
Allah establishes the truth through His words despite the criminals' dislike.
Allah separates corrupt from good and consigns the corrupt to Hell, a general account of final sorting and loss.
A cry in truth destroys wrongdoers and leaves them as debris, a broad image of decisive divine reversal.
The ruined town and Allah's restoration demonstrate power over collapse and death, though not the focus's core claim.
The Quran is sent down with truth and the Messenger as bearer of good news and warning, broadly framing divine recompense.
Allah alone owns the heavens and earth, and apart from Him there is neither protector nor helper.
Allah is the Protector of believers, bringing them from darkness into light.
For the God-conscious, what is with Allah is better and includes the beautiful final return.
Allah is the Protector of the believers, directly naming the believing relation of guardianship.
When two groups considered failing, Allah was their Protector and believers are commanded to rely on Him.
If Allah aids you none can overcome you, and if He forsakes you no one can help after Him.
Allah is sufficient as Protector and sufficient as Helper.
Allah possesses the reward of this world and the Hereafter, joining present and final recompense under His control.
Allah gives believers their full rewards, while those who reject His worship find no protector or helper apart from Him.
The verse directly identifies Allah as the believers' Protector, alongside the Messenger and faithful community.
Those who take Allah as Protector belong to the party that will prevail.
The speaker declares Allah his Protector, the Revealer of the Book who protects the righteous.
Allah is the believers' Master, the excellent Master and excellent Helper.
Allah gives believers glad tidings of mercy, pleasure, and gardens containing enduring great reward.
Believers say Allah is their Master and place their trust in Him.
Allah's pleasure is declared greater than the promised gardens, refining the measure of the best reward.
Allah alone gives life and death, and apart from Him people have neither protector nor helper.
No one can remove harm Allah decrees or repel the grace He gives, confirming His unshared decisive authority.
Joseph calls Allah his Protector in this world and the Hereafter and asks for a righteous final joining.
Those who believe and do good have blessedness and an excellent final homecoming.
The Quran guides to what is most upright and promises the believers who do good a great reward.
Whoever Allah leaves astray will find no protector apart from Him.
Allah has no partner in dominion and no protecting ally arising from weakness.
Whomever Allah leaves astray will never find a rightly guiding protector.
Those who take Allah's servants as protectors besides Him are warned of the futility of that allegiance.
Those who believe and do righteous deeds receive the gardens of Paradise as their lodging.
Their abiding Paradise, from which they seek no transfer, displays the lasting quality of the true outcome.
Whoever comes to Allah as a believing righteous worker receives the highest ranks.
Eternal gardens are given as the reward of the one purified, directly connecting righteous preparation with final recompense.
Allah is the believers' Master, the excellent Master and excellent Helper.
None can escape Allah, and apart from Him there is no protector or helper.
Apart from Allah there is no protector or intercessor, after He created and governs all things.
No one can shield people from Allah's harm or withhold His mercy, limiting every rival claim to protection.
Those who seek Allah, His Messenger, and the Hereafter are promised a great reward.
Allah's greeting to believers on the Day they meet Him is peace, and He has prepared a noble reward.
Allah gives righteous reciters their full rewards and increases them from His bounty.
The patient are given their reward without measure, illuminating the focus's preference for divine recompense.
Allah's sufficiency for His servant counters fear generated by alleged protectors besides Him.
All intercession belongs to Allah, whose dominion and final return exclude independent protective power.
Allah judges with truth, whereas those invoked apart from Him judge nothing.
On the day of turning away, none can protect from Allah; whom Allah leaves astray has no guide.
Allah is the true Protector; He gives life to the dead and has power over all things.
People cannot escape Allah on earth and have no protector or helper apart from Him.
Those punished have no protectors to help them apart from Allah.
Allah is the Protector of the God-conscious, unlike the false protectorship among wrongdoers.
Allah is the Master of believers, while the disbelievers have no master.
Allah promises forgiveness and a great reward to the believers who do righteous deeds.
Whoever lends Allah a goodly loan receives it multiplied and has a noble reward.
Those who believe in Allah and His messengers have their reward and light with their Lord.
The call to race toward forgiveness and Paradise presents Allah's bounty as the decisive final gain.
On the Day of Gathering, Allah admits believers who do good into gardens; that is the great success.
Allah removes the evil of the God-conscious person's deeds and magnifies that person's reward.
Allah is the Prophet's Master, with Gabriel and the righteous believers supporting by His leave.
The question of who can protect disbelievers from painful punishment underscores Allah's exclusive power.
No one can protect the Messenger from Allah, and no refuge exists apart from Him.
The righteous receive this as their reward, and their effort is accepted.
The reward from the Lord is presented as an abundant gift in the final judgment scene.
Believers who do righteous deeds receive an unfailing reward.
Believers who do righteous deeds have an unending reward.
Their reward with their Lord is eternal gardens, joined with Allah's pleasure and their pleasure in Him.
Those who believe have the abode of peace with their Lord, and He is their Protector because of their deeds.
The command to follow what Allah revealed forbids taking protectors besides Him.
Moses addresses Allah as the community's Protector and seeks His forgiveness and mercy.
Those called apart from Allah cannot help their followers or even help themselves.
Allah's devoted allies have no fear and will not grieve, showing the security of true guardianship.
Those who incline toward wrongdoing face the Fire and have no protectors apart from Allah.
The verse challenges taking protectors apart from Allah and contrasts blindness with sight and darkness with light.
It rebukes taking Iblis and his offspring as protectors instead of Allah, an explicit false-allegiance contrast.
False objects of worship disclaim taking protectors besides Allah, exposing the error of such dependence.
Those who take protectors apart from Allah are compared to one relying on the frailest of homes.
Those who affirm Allah receive angelic reassurance not to fear or grieve, with Paradise promised as their final reward.
The angels declare themselves protectors of believers in this world and the Hereafter by Allah's provision.
Allah relieves despair with mercy and is named the Protector, the Praiseworthy.
The Fire is called the disbelievers' assigned master after every ransom fails, a stark contrast to Allah as true Master.
